item.title: What Are Those Funny Little Bumps Trying to Tell You?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Dog warts are benign growths that can be caused by canine papillomavirus (CPV), with 24 different types now identified — most affecting either the skin or the mouth, and most resolving on their own without any medical intervention
  • Puppies and adolescent dogs are most commonly affected because their immune systems are still learning to recognize new viruses, while senior dogs may develop slower-growing skin warts as immune function naturally declines with age and with hormone changes
  • The classic papilloma-type dog wart has a rough cauliflower texture, appears in clusters or singly around the mouth, eyes, face, paws, or ears, and usually resolves within four to eight weeks for oral warts and about three months for skin warts
  • Canine papillomavirus is species-specific — dogs cannot pass it to cats, other pets, or humans, and the virus typically enters through tiny skin breaks or moist areas like the mouth
  • Integrative and holistic veterinarians focus on supporting the immune system with real-food diets, gut health, immune-supportive nutrients, medicinal mushrooms, stress reduction, and homeopathic remedies rather than jumping to invasive interventions

You are scratching your dog's chin one afternoon and your fingers find something new — a small, rough bump that was not there last week. It looks a little like a tiny cauliflower, and it does not seem to bother them. You check for more, and see another one on their lip, and a third on their paw — so what are these unusual growths?

There is a good chance you are looking at a viral wart. And while any new lump on your dog deserves attention, the good news is that most of these particular bumps are far more of a cosmetic issue than a medical crisis. They are actually your dog's immune system sending a signal — and once you understand what they are, they become much less alarming.

What These Bumps Actually Are

Viral dog warts are benign growths caused by canine papillomavirus (CPV). Researchers have now identified 24 different types of canine papillomavirus, most of which affect either the skin or the mouth. Cats have their own version, feline papillomavirus, with six types identified so far. Both species carry papillomaviruses commonly, though visible warts are far more frequent in dogs than cats.1

The virus works by entering skin cells through tiny breaks — a small cut from rough play, a scratch from grass, a naturally moist area like the mouth — and hijacking normal cell growth to create the characteristic bumpy texture we recognize as a wart. The immune system then gradually recognizes the invader and mounts a response, which is what eventually clears the wart.2

Who Gets Them and Why

Cutaneous warts are actually the second most frequent skin tumor in dogs under one year of age. Puppies and adolescent dogs are the classic patients because their immune systems are still learning to recognize new viruses, and their tendency to mouth and chew everything in sight gives the virus plenty of entry points. Oral warts in particular tend to show up in dogs under about 18 months.3

Older dogs — usually over about seven years — also develop warts, though a different flavor of them. These warts tend to show up on the body and tend to not be papillomavirus related; they are generally sebaceous adenomas, benign growths stemming out of the sebaceous gland. Their warts tend to be slower-growing skin warts rather than the classic oral clusters, and they show up as pet's experience age-related changes in skin barrier health, hormone balance, and immune function.

Certain breeds may be more susceptible to papillomavirus based on various meta-analyses of case reports and geographic studies: Pugs and Miniature Schnauzers are known to be predisposed to the viral cutaneous plaque form of papillomavirus, and case reports of this in Vizslas have emerged. Other breeds including again Miniature Schnauzers and Labrador retrievers have been reported to be predisposed to the papillomatous form of the disease.

Anything that suppresses immune function — chronic stress, poor diet, illness, being on immunosuppressive medication — makes any dog more vulnerable regardless of breed. And in females, hormonal changes such as coming into heat for the first time can also lower immune resilience temporarily.4

What They Look Like

The classic dog wart has a rough, cauliflower-like texture that feels firm to the touch. They can appear as single growths or in clusters, and they range from the size of a grain of rice to the size of a small grape. Some look feathery or scaly, and the color usually matches your dog's skin — flesh-toned, pink, or slightly darker. Common places to find them include:

  • Mouth, lips, and gums (especially in puppies)
  • Around the eyes and eyelids
  • On the face and muzzle
  • Ears and ear flaps
  • Between the toes and on paw pads
  • Occasionally on the genital area

Fresh warts often appear pink or flesh-colored. Older ones may darken or develop a crusty surface as the immune system begins fighting back. Warts on the mouth deserve a little extra attention since they can sometimes interfere with eating in severe cases, but this is uncommon.5

How They Spread

The virus spreads through direct contact — saliva, shared toys, food and water bowls, bedding — with an infected dog or with a dog who is carrying the virus without symptoms. Inoculation of the virus requires a microtear or injury in the skin surface for the virus to transfer. The incubation period is typically four to six weeks, which means a wart you are spotting today came from an exposure over a month ago. That timeline is actually reassuring: the situation is not an immediate emergency, and your dog's immune system has already been working on it for weeks.

The species boundary is important to know. Canine papillomavirus affects only dogs. Your cats, your family members, and other pets in the household are not at risk of catching it from your dog. Feline papillomavirus works the same way — cats cannot give it to dogs, and neither species passes it to humans.6,7

The Reassuring Part

Most canine cutaneous warts regress spontaneously within about three months, and most oral warts resolve within four to eight weeks. From an integrative and holistic veterinary perspective, the appearance of warts is often best understood as a sign that your dog's immune system is actively engaging with and building resistance to the virus — much the way children develop resistance to common viruses as they grow. Progression from a benign wart to something more serious like a squamous cell carcinoma is extremely rare, and typically only happens in dogs with significant immune suppression.8,9

Warts may actually appear to worsen slightly before improvement begins — this represents immune activation, not treatment failure. During the first couple of weeks you may see little visible change. Significant improvement usually shows up during weeks 5 through 7, with complete resolution by around week 8 in most straightforward cases.

Supporting Your Dog's Immune Response

Since a strong immune system is what actually clears the virus, the most useful thing you can do is support that system. Integrative and holistic veterinarians commonly focus on:10

  • Species-appropriate diet — High-quality, minimally processed, real-food feeding — with plenty of clean protein, healthy fats, and appropriate carbohydrates — provides the raw materials your dog's immune system uses to build defenses. Fresh food matters more than most pet parents realize when it comes to immune resilience.
  • Gut health support — A significant portion of the immune system lives in the gut. A good-quality probiotic and prebiotic combination, along with digestive enzymes if needed, can help keep the immune foundation strong.
  • Immune-supportive nutrients — Vitamin C, vitamin D at appropriate levels, EPA and DHA, and chlorella are all commonly used in holistic protocols. A methyl donor like DMG (dimethylglycine) or SAMe is sometimes added. Talk to an integrative vet about supplements and doses appropriate for your specific dog.
  • Medicinal mushrooms — Extracts like maitake D-fraction, reishi, and turkey tail are widely used to support immune modulation in dogs. Look for veterinary-grade formulations rather than human supplements.
  • Stress reduction — Emotional, physical, and environmental stressors all suppress immune function. A calm household routine, plenty of rest, appropriate exercise, and time outdoors all matter. Even minor adjustments — reducing loud noises during recovery, keeping feeding schedules predictable — can help.
  • Homeopathic support — Many holistic veterinarians reach for constitutional homeopathic remedies matched to the specific dog's overall symptom picture, rather than a generic wart remedy. Working with a veterinary homeopath can produce genuinely impressive results for some dogs.

Home Care While You Wait

A few practical things can help while the immune system does its work. None of them will make the warts vanish overnight, but they do prevent the small problems that can turn a straightforward viral wart into a bigger issue:

  • Discourage licking, chewing, or scratching at wart sites — the trauma can introduce bacteria and slow healing
  • Do a gentle daily check for changes in size, color, or new growths
  • Clean any discharge around a wart site gently with warm water
  • Consider weekly photos in similar lighting to track real progress objectively
  • Separate food and water bowls, toys, and bedding from other dogs in the household during the active wart phase
  • Continue normal exercise, play, and socialization — strict isolation is not necessary or helpful
  • If your dog is a persistent licker, a soft recovery collar worn briefly during unsupervised time prevents wart trauma without adding stress

When to Call the Vet

Most warts do not need medical intervention. But there are situations that warrant a professional look, such as:

  • A bump that is smooth and dome-shaped, unusually hard or soft, or growing rapidly over days rather than weeks
  • Signs of pain when the area is touched
  • Bleeding, discharge, warmth, or swelling around the growth
  • Warts that interfere with eating, drinking, or breathing
  • Warts that persist well beyond the typical eight-to-twelve-week window without any sign of improvement
  • Any lump you are not confident is a wart — sebaceous cysts, mast cell tumors, and other skin conditions can look similar and require different management

In dogs with severe cases — usually those on immunosuppressive medication or with widespread oral warts that are interfering with eating — veterinarians occasionally use specific interventions to speed resolution. But for the vast majority of otherwise healthy dogs, patience plus immune support does the job.

What the Bumps Are Really Saying

Those funny little cauliflower bumps are not nothing. They are a signal that your dog encountered a virus, and their immune system is now doing exactly what it is supposed to do. In most cases, they will come, they will persist for a few weeks, and they will disappear again with the immune system slightly stronger and better educated than it was before. Support the immune system with real food, a low-stress environment, and thoughtful integrative care, and the whole process usually resolves quietly on its own.

Keep an eye on them, take a picture now and then to track progress, and check in with your veterinarian — ideally one with an integrative or holistic bent — if anything looks off. But mostly, take a deep breath. Your dog is doing exactly what their body was built to do. Sometimes, the funny little bumps are just proof that everything is working.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,7,9 Front. Vet. Sci., 16 May 2023, Volume 10 - 2023
  • 2,4,6,8,10 Best Life 4 Pets, December 21, 2025
  • 5,11 Dogs Naturally Magazine, November 9, 2021

item.title: Scared Rescue Dog Finally Discovers the Joy of Toys
item.description:
Marshall was so frightened when rescuers found him that he wouldn't even take a treat. After weeks of patience, he finally felt safe enough to play with his first toy. Now, he lights up around other dogs and is waiting for a forever home with a canine best friend.

item.title: How Spaying and Neutering Influences Cancer and Disease Risk
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Studies show that spaying/neutering large and giant breed dogs increases the risk for many diseases, including several types of canine cancer
  • While animal health groups are reconsidering their position on automatic spays/neuters, animal welfare groups understandably remain firmly on the side of early spays or neuters for all shelter pets
  • A reasonable compromise may exist in broader use of sterilization procedures that do not remove the ovaries or testes
  • If you’re considering, for example, an ovary-sparing spay for a female dog or a vasectomy for a male, resources exist but aren’t widely available
  • If you decide to spay/neuter your large or giant breed dog, consider waiting until your pet reaches musculoskeletal maturity, and in the case of a female dog, wait until she’s completed her second estrus cycle before scheduling the surgery

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published November 13, 2019.

There’s a growing body of research that indicates spaying and neutering dogs, especially large and giant breeds, and especially at an early age, increases the risk for a wide range of long-term health problems, as outlined in the following table:

Animal Health vs. Animal Welfare

Given the mounting evidence that spay/neuter may not be appropriate in every instance, animal health organizations such as the Morris Animal Foundation and the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA)1 have begun to back away from the 1970s-era orthodoxy that called for early spay/neuter for every pet in the U.S.

Back then, both veterinarians and responsible pet owners signed on wholeheartedly to the spay/neuter movement out of a genuine desire to help solve the terrible problem of unwanted pets, tens of millions of which were euthanized in shelters each year.

Today, 31 states and the District of Columbia require that pets adopted from shelters be spayed or neutered before they leave the facility, or that adopters contractually agree to have the procedure performed within a certain timeframe.2 The ASPCA (American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) and other animal welfare organizations also advocate early desexing of all companion animals.

To animal welfare groups charged with managing unwanted pets, the current spay/neuter strategy makes sense. They are necessarily focused on the big picture, and the most effective way to reduce the homeless pet population is to prevent pregnancy. Whereas individual pet owners only have to make sterilization decisions for the dogs in their care, animal welfare organizations have to make those decisions on a much larger scale, for the good of the many rather than the few.

A Potential Compromise: Sterilization Without Desexing

The reason, in simple terms, that spays/neuters can cause long-term health problems is because these procedures remove the hormone-producing gonads (ovaries or testes). These hormones are used by the body in a multitude of important ways — especially in the case of young animals. Removing the gonads removes dogs’ ability to make these very important naturally occurring substances.

Spays and neuters are desexing procedures (i.e., they remove the animal’s ability to produce sex hormones) used primarily for purposes of sterilization to prevent pregnancy. What many pet owners don’t realize, and veterinarians aren’t taught in vet school, is that dogs can be sterilized without being desexed.

For example, female dogs can undergo a modified spay, also called an ovary-sparing spay or hysterectomy (vs. ovariohysterectomy) that removes the uterus but leaves the ovaries in place, and male dogs can have vasectomies that preserve the testes. Both procedures result in sterilization, but without removing the gonads and the hormones they produce. There is also a zinc injection that can render male dogs sterile but still allows for a small amount of hormones to be produced.

Ovary-Sparing Spay

Because the ovaries are preserved in modified spays, female dogs continue to have estrous cycles (go into heat), but since the uterus has been removed, there’s no bloody discharge. However, the vulva does enlarge. In addition, females continue to secrete pheromones that are attractive to male dogs, and they are receptive to males during their cycles.

It’s recommended that female dogs who’ve undergone ovary-sparing spays not be allowed to mate while in heat, for post-surgery anatomical reasons that may increase the risk of vaginal trauma. You can read more about ovary-sparing spays at the Parsemus Foundation.

Vasectomy

The Parsemus Foundation also provides information on vasectomies for male dogs:

“Although it is not widely performed, vasectomy is an accepted way to sterilize dogs without impacting hormones. A number of veterinarians are willing to offer vasectomy (for example, for clients who want to sterilize their dogs right away to prevent accidental litters, but wait for neuter until after the dogs’ growth plates close). We are gathering a list of veterinarians who offer vasectomy.
If you choose vasectomy for your dog, be sure to ask the vet to look into current recommendations for human vasectomy techniques, as some techniques have been shown to be more effective than others (such as cautery with fascial interposition) and are now considered best practice.”3

Unfortunately, only full spays and neuters are taught in U.S. veterinary schools, so there are relatively few veterinarians across the country who have learned alternative techniques. Please take a minute to email your state veterinary teaching hospital (if you have one) or the AVMA and ask that students be taught alternative techniques while in vet school. The good news is that the Parsemus Foundation has compiled a state-by-state list of veterinarians who do provide such services at this link.

Be sure to read the information at the top of the page before searching for a vet in your area. Other potential resources include the Facebook Ovary Sparing Spay and Vasectomy Info Group and the Society of Theriogenology.

Sterilization Recommendations

The recommended approach is to work with each individual pet parent to make decisions that will provide the most health benefits for the dog. Whenever possible, leaving dogs intact is preferred. However, this approach requires a highly responsible pet guardian who is fully committed to and capable of preventing the dog from mating (unless the owner is a responsible breeder and that's the goal).

It’s important to note that the adoption of intact shelter animals isn’t advocated for people who may or may not be responsible pet owners. Shelter veterinarians don't have the time or resources to build a relationship with every adoptive family, so the animals in their care need to be sterilized prior to adoption to prevent more litters of unwanted pets.

The second choice is to sterilize without desexing so the testes or ovaries can continue to produce hormones essential for the dog's health and well-being.

Rarely, older, intact male dogs develop moderate to severe benign prostatic hyperplasia (an enlarged prostate) that may be improved with conventional neutering. Generally speaking, mature intact dogs have had the benefit of a lifetime of sex hormone production, so the endocrine imbalances seen with spayed or neutered puppies don't occur when dogs are desexed in their later years.

Unfortunately, as noted earlier, veterinary schools in the U.S. only teach full spays and neuters, so unless your own vet has obtained additional training in sterilization techniques that spare the ovaries or testicles (which is unlikely), you may have only one option available to sterilize your pet. In that case, it’s best to wait until your dog has reached full musculoskeletal maturity, and if you have a female, to also wait until she’s completed her second estrus cycle before scheduling the surgery.

Sources and References

  • 1 The Atlantic, July 22, 2019
  • 2 AVMA.org, Updated June 2019 (Archived)
  • 3 Parsemus Foundation

What many pet owners don’t realize, and veterinarians aren’t taught in vet school, is that dogs can be sterilized without being desexed.

For example, female dogs can undergo a modified spay, also called an ovary-sparing spay or hysterectomy (vs. ovariohysterectomy) that removes the uterus but leaves the ovaries in place, and male dogs can have vasectomies that preserve the testes. Both procedures result in sterilization, but without removing the gonads and the hormones they produce. There is also a zinc injection that can render male dogs sterile but still allows for a small amount of hormones to be produced.

Ovary-Sparing Spay

Because the ovaries are preserved in modified spays, female dogs continue to have estrous cycles (go into heat), but since the uterus has been removed, there’s no bloody discharge. However, the vulva does enlarge. In addition, females continue to secrete pheromones that are attractive to male dogs, and they are receptive to males during their cycles.

It’s recommended that female dogs who’ve undergone ovary-sparing spays not be allowed to mate while in heat, for post-surgery anatomical reasons that may increase the risk of vaginal trauma. You can read more about ovary-sparing spays at the Parsemus Foundation.

Vasectomy

The Parsemus Foundation also provides information on vasectomies for male dogs:

“Although it is not widely performed, vasectomy is an accepted way to sterilize dogs without impacting hormones. A number of veterinarians are willing to offer vasectomy (for example, for clients who want to sterilize their dogs right away to prevent accidental litters, but wait for neuter until after the dogs’ growth plates close). We are gathering a list of veterinarians who offer vasectomy.
If you choose vasectomy for your dog, be sure to ask the vet to look into current recommendations for human vasectomy techniques, as some techniques have been shown to be more effective than others (such as cautery with fascial interposition) and are now considered best practice.”3

Unfortunately, only full spays and neuters are taught in U.S. veterinary schools, so there are relatively few veterinarians across the country who have learned alternative techniques. Please take a minute to email your state veterinary teaching hospital (if you have one) or the AVMA and ask that students be taught alternative techniques while in vet school. The good news is that the Parsemus Foundation has compiled a state-by-state list of veterinarians who do provide such services at this link.

Be sure to read the information at the top of the page before searching for a vet in your area. Other potential resources include the Facebook Ovary Sparing Spay and Vasectomy Info Group and the Society of Theriogenology.

Sterilization Recommendations

The recommended approach is to work with each individual pet parent to make decisions that will provide the most health benefits for the dog. Whenever possible, leaving dogs intact is preferred. However, this approach requires a highly responsible pet guardian who is fully committed to and capable of preventing the dog from mating (unless the owner is a responsible breeder and that's the goal).

It’s important to note that the adoption of intact shelter animals isn’t advocated for people who may or may not be responsible pet owners. Shelter veterinarians don't have the time or resources to build a relationship with every adoptive family, so the animals in their care need to be sterilized prior to adoption to prevent more litters of unwanted pets.

The second choice is to sterilize without desexing so the testes or ovaries can continue to produce hormones essential for the dog's health and well-being.

Rarely, older, intact male dogs develop moderate to severe benign prostatic hyperplasia (an enlarged prostate) that may be improved with conventional neutering. Generally speaking, mature intact dogs have had the benefit of a lifetime of sex hormone production, so the endocrine imbalances seen with spayed or neutered puppies don't occur when dogs are desexed in their later years.

Unfortunately, as noted earlier, veterinary schools in the U.S. only teach full spays and neuters, so unless your own vet has obtained additional training in sterilization techniques that spare the ovaries or testicles (which is unlikely), you may have only one option available to sterilize your pet. In that case, it’s best to wait until your dog has reached full musculoskeletal maturity, and if you have a female, to also wait until she’s completed her second estrus cycle before scheduling the surgery.

item.title: Your Next Chapter Could Use a 4-Legged Sidekick
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Research shows adults 60 and older who own pets are 36% less likely to consider themselves lonely, with dog ownership also linked to lower blood pressure, better cardiovascular health, and improved cognitive function
  • Age matters less than lifestyle when choosing a dog — the right fit depends on exercise capability, training experience, living situation, financial readiness, and physical ability to walk and groom the dog
  • Easygoing breeds like Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, Shih Tzus, Pugs, French Bulldogs, Coton de Tulears, and Havanese suit seniors who prefer moderate exercise and lots of snuggle time
  • Active seniors may thrive with Bichon Frisés, Pembroke Welsh Corgis, English Cocker Spaniels, Dachshunds, Beagles, Boston Terriers, or Poodles — breeds that reward regular walks with better behavior at home
  • Consider adopting an adult or senior dog for a known personality and settled temperament, and always have a backup caregiver plan in place for the years ahead — many small breeds live 12 to 16 years or more

Life shifts as the years go by. Maybe the kids have long since moved out, and the house feels a little too quiet in the afternoons. Maybe you have retired, downsized, or just find yourself with more time on your hands and fewer built-in reasons to leave the front porch. There is a compelling body of research — and a lot of very happy pet parents in their 60s, 70s, and beyond — suggesting that this might be exactly the right chapter to bring a dog into your life.

Why a Dog May Be Just What You Need

The benefits of dog ownership stack up in ways that hit exactly what tends to slip in older age. In one study of adults 60 years or older,1 pet parents were 36% less likely to consider themselves lonely than non-pet parents. Dogs give you a reason to get up in the morning, a warm presence throughout the day, and a built-in conversation starter every time you take them out.2

Beyond the emotional piece, the health benefits are real. Dog ownership has been associated with lower stress levels, reduced blood pressure, better cardiovascular health, more consistent daily exercise, and even reduced risk of death due to heart disease.3

Petting a dog releases endorphins and can lower your heart rate on the spot. Walking a dog twice a day builds an exercise habit almost automatically. And the responsibility of caring for another living being — feeding, grooming, keeping an eye on their well-being — has been shown to help support cognitive function in older adults.4,5,6

For seniors living alone, in a quiet neighborhood, or in a senior community, a dog often becomes the single most consistent source of warmth, structure, and joy in the day. That is not sentimental language — it is what the research keeps showing.

Questions to Ask Yourself First

Age itself matters less than lifestyle and physical ability. A 68-year-old avid hiker and a 68-year-old who prefers reading in the recliner need very different dogs. Before you commit, run through a few honest questions:

  • How much daily exercise are you realistically up for — and enjoy?
  • Do you have experience training dogs, or would you want a breed that is easy to train?
  • Can you comfortably walk, lift, and groom the size of dog you are considering?
  • What is your living situation — house with a yard, apartment, senior community with a pet policy?
  • Do you travel often, and would you want your dog to come with you?
  • Will you have grandchildren visiting? A kid-friendly temperament matters.
  • Have you thought about who would care for your dog if you were unable — a family member, friend, or plan in place?
  • Can you comfortably cover the ongoing costs — food, veterinary care, grooming, boarding, supplies?

None of these are dealbreakers. They are just the practical realities that shape which breed will make you a very happy dog owner instead of an overwhelmed one.

Great Breeds for Easygoing Days

If your ideal afternoon involves a short walk followed by a snuggle on the couch, these breeds tend to be right at home. Most are small enough to lift comfortably, quiet enough for shared walls, and content with modest exercise, which makes them especially good matches for apartment living, senior communities, or anyone whose energy comes and goes throughout the day:7,8,9

  • Cavalier King Charles Spaniel — Probably the most-recommended breed for seniors. Warm, affectionate, gentle, and content with moderate exercise. Natural cuddler with soulful eyes.
  • Shih Tzu — A solid little dog (up to 16 pounds) bred as royal companions. Low exercise needs, friendly with grandchildren, and happy in an apartment.
  • Pug — Comical, affectionate, and low-key. Loves lounging with their humans (which means watching their weight matters). Playful with kids.
  • French Bulldog — The most popular AKC breed for several years running. Adaptable, quiet, and comfortable in smaller spaces.
  • Coton de Tulear — Cheerful, low-shedding, and easy to train. Adapts well to travel and can live 15 to 19 years, which is one of the longer lifespans in small breeds.
  • Havanese — The only breed native to Cuba. Quiet, cheerful, patient with children, and happy with short walks and lots of snuggle time.
  • Pomeranian — Tiny (under 7 pounds), smart, and easy to train. Content with indoor games and short walks.
  • Yorkshire Terrier — This breed is loving and outgoing but can be stubborn, so training experience helps.

Great Breeds for Active Seniors

If you are the retiree who is out at 6 a.m. for a walk in the park, thinking about hiking trips with the grandkids, or looking for a dog to keep pace with your energy, look at these breeds. They bring more energy, curiosity, and drive than the classic lap dogs, but they are still manageable for older adults who enjoy a real daily routine:10,11,12

  • Bichon Frisé — Curly-coated, hypoallergenic, playful, and lively. A great fit for active seniors who want a companion for both couch time and outings.
  • Pembroke Welsh Corgi — Around 30 pounds of muscle in a small package. Athletic and famously charming (Queen Elizabeth owned 30 of them), but they can be heavy shedders and need frequent brushing.
  • English Cocker Spaniel — Medium-sized, lively, quick learner, and happy with a couple of 30-minute walks a day. Good traveler and loves being wherever you are. This breed does need careful grooming to manage their silky coat and allergy prone skin.
  • Dachshund — Small but spirited, comes in standard and miniature sizes with three coat types. Low grooming needs; short walks are ideal because they are prone to back problems, and this is not a breed made for jumping on and off the bed or navigating steep stairs.
  • Italian Greyhound — Playful, graceful, and lap-loving. Requires regular exercise and appreciates a sweater in chilly weather.
  • Beagle — Friendly, energetic, and motivating for owners who want a dog that will insist on daily walks. This is a breed known for baying, so noise can be a limitation.
  • Boston Terrier — Affectionate, adaptable, and trainable. Great for small apartments. Some respiratory limits in hot weather.
  • Poodle (Standard, Miniature, or Toy) — Intelligent, trainable, hypoallergenic, and adaptable to almost any living situation.

Should You Get a Puppy or an Adult Dog?

This is one of the bigger decisions. Puppies are adorable, but they are also a full-time commitment for the first year or so — housebreaking, chewing, midnight potty breaks, obedience training, and enough energy to test anyone's patience. If you are up for it, a puppy grows into exactly the dog you shape.

For most older adults, an adult or senior dog is often a better fit. They come already housebroken and leash-trained, their personalities are settled so you know what you are getting, and their energy tends to be more predictable. Adopting an older dog from a shelter or breed-specific rescue also gives a home to a dog who needs one — and older dogs are frequently overlooked in shelters despite being some of the loveliest companions available.

Adopting Versus Buying

While reputable breeders can help match you with the right temperament, screen for breed-specific health issues, and answer questions about lifespan and care over the years, it is highly recommended to check your local animal shelter first. Local shelters are full of loving, pure and mixed breeds pets that are waiting for their forever home. Plus, their personalities are already known, and many of them are the exact easygoing lap-dog temperaments that suit older adults perfectly.

In addition, make sure to spend time with the dog before committing. Personality varies within every breed. The right fit is not just about breed characteristics — it is about the specific dog in front of you.

Planning for the Long Haul

A responsible piece of getting a dog at this stage of life is thinking beyond today. Small dogs commonly live 12 to 16 years — some longer. Consider:

  • Who would care for the dog if you had a health event or were unable for a stretch?
  • Is there a family member, neighbor, or friend committed to helping if needed?
  • If you might move into senior living or assisted care, are you looking at pet-friendly options? Many facilities allow pets but have size, weight, or type restrictions.
  • Financial planning for veterinary care, grooming, boarding, and supplies over the dog's lifetime.
  • A simple written plan for what happens to your dog if you are unable to care for them, shared with the person who would step in.

None of this should stop you. It is just good planning, and it makes the dog's future secure regardless of what happens.

A Companion for the Chapter Ahead

The research keeps landing in the same place. Dog ownership in later life is associated with less loneliness, more physical activity, better mood, sharper cognition, lower blood pressure, and a richer daily experience. And beyond the studies, there is the simple daily reality — a warm body curled up next to you in the evening, a wagging tail meeting you at the door, and someone who genuinely delights in every small thing you do together.

Whether you pick a Cavalier King Charles Spaniel for lap-dog snuggles, a Pembroke Welsh Corgi for morning walks with attitude, or a mixed-breed rescue whose story finds you when you visit the shelter, the right dog can turn what might be a quieter chapter of life into one of the fullest. Talk to your doctor if you have health questions, talk to your vet about which breeds fit your situation, and talk to shelters and rescues about who is waiting for you. Your next chapter could genuinely use a four-legged sidekick. And there is a very good chance one is already looking for you.

Sources and References

  • 1 Aging Ment Health. 2014; 18(3): 394–399
  • 2,4,9,12 American Kennel Club, August 17, 2026
  • 3 Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and OutcomesVolume 12, Number 10, October 8, 2019
  • 5,8,11 LTC News, June 13, 2023
  • 6 Sci Rep. 2023 Sep 7;13:14738. doi: 10.1038/s41598-023-41813-y
  • 7,10 Good Housekeeping, September 9, 2026

item.title: Still Common in the US, yet Banned in Several Countries — Why Is This Happening?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Declawing of cats is still legal in the U.S., and sadly, it’s still somewhat common
  • It’s important to understand that declawing is not nail removal, it’s the permanent amputation of bones in each of your cat’s toes
  • A study concluded that declawed cats have more pain and behavior issues than non-declawed cats
  • The study’s authors hope their results will encourage veterinarians to reconsider declawing cats
  • There are many alternatives to declawing your cat, starting with providing appropriate scratching surfaces and training kitty to use them

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published August 15, 2017.

Many articles have been written here at Healthy Pets about the inhumane practice of declawing cats, a procedure called an onychectomy. The surgery has been banned in several countries, but continues to be commonly and legally performed in many others, including the U.S.

It’s Not Declawing, It’s ‘De-Toeing’

Cats use their claws for balance, exercise and stretching and toning the muscles of their legs, back, shoulders and paws. They also use them to hunt and capture prey, to escape or defend against predators and as part of their marking behavior when they live outdoors. What many people don’t realize is that declawing isn't a nail trim, or even nail removal. It's not even declawing, it's "de-toeing." The procedure removes not just the claws, but also the bones, nerves, joint capsule, collateral ligaments and the extensor or flexor tendons.

Cats are digitigrades, meaning they walk on their toes. Most other mammals, including humans, walk on the soles of their feet. Cats have three bones in each of their toes, just as humans have three bones in each of their fingers — two joints and three bones. A kitty's claw actually grows out of the last bone. This is very different from human fingernails, which grow out of flesh. Since a cat’s nail grows from the bone, it’s the bone that has to be amputated to prevent the claw from growing back.

The declawing procedure involves cutting between the second and third bones, and amputating the last bone that contains the claw. This severs everything in the way — nerves, tendons and blood vessels. A front-paw declaw requires 10 separate amputations. If the hind paws are also done, that's eight more separate amputations. Thankfully, hind paw declawing is much less common, but also much more painful for the cat.

Past research into the effects of declawing has primarily focused on short-term, post-operative changes. But in 2017, a small team of researchers from the U.S. and Canada published the results of a study to determine whether declawing increases the risk of long-term pain and unwanted behaviors in cats.1

Pain is actually very often the root cause of undesirable behaviors such as eliminating outside the litterbox and aggression, including biting. This situation is obviously harmful for the cat who’s in constant pain, and it’s risky for human family members who may be bitten. In addition, litterbox avoidance and aggression are two very common reasons pet parents give for relinquishing their cats to shelters.

63% of Declawed Study Cats Had Residual Bone Fragments

For the retrospective study, the researchers looked at 137 non-declawed cats and 137 declawed cats, 33 of which were declawed on both the front and back paws. Of the 274 kitties, 176 were privately owned (88 declawed, 88 non-declawed) and 98 were shelter cats (49 declawed and 49 non-declawed).

All the cats underwent physical exams to check for signs of pain and “barbering,” which is excessive licking and/or chewing of fur. In addition, their medical records for the previous two years were reviewed for reported unwanted behaviors such as inappropriate elimination, aggression and biting with minimal provocation.

X-rays of the declawed cats were also taken to check for distal limb abnormalities, including P3 (third phalanx) bone fragments. Sadly, well over half (86% or 63%) of these kitties showed radiographic evidence of residual P3 fragments.

Declawed Cats Had Significantly More Pain and Behavior Issues Than Non-Declawed Cats

The research team discovered that inappropriate elimination, biting, aggression and over-grooming occurred much more often in the declawed than the non-declawed kitties. The declawed cats had seven times the litterbox issues, four times the biting behavior and three times the aggressive and over-grooming behaviors as their non-declawed counterparts.

The declawed kitties also had almost three times the back pain of the non-declawed cats, which the researchers theorized could be the result of altered gait due to the shortening of the declawed limbs, and/or persistent pain at the surgery site, which causes compensatory weight shift to the pelvic limbs.

When an onychectomy is performed, the veterinarian is supposed to remove the entire third phalanx (P3) bone per the surgical guidelines set forth by the Diplomates of the American College of Veterinary Surgeons. The fact that 86 of the 137 declawed cats were walking around with P3 bone fragments means a significant number of vets aren’t performing declawing procedures up to standard.

These cats had even more back pain and undesirable behaviors than the remaining declawed cats, but the researchers also make the point that even when onychectomy is performed to standard, it doesn’t eliminate the risks. Residual pain in the declawed toes prompts many cats to look for soft surfaces rather than litter for purposes of elimination.

The researchers also explained that painful declawed cats may resort to biting when touched because their first line of defense, their claws, has been taken from them. Lead study author Nicole Martell-Moran, a veterinarian at a cat-only clinic in Houston, told EurekAlert:

“The result of this research reinforces my opinion that declawed cats with unwanted behaviors may not be ‘bad cats,’ they may simply need pain management. We now have scientific evidence that declawing is more detrimental to our feline patients than we originally thought and I hope this study becomes one of many that will lead veterinarians to reconsider declawing cats.”2

5 Ways to Minimize Cat Claw Damage Around Your Home

It’s Not Declawing, It’s ‘De-Toeing’

Cats use their claws for balance, exercise and stretching and toning the muscles of their legs, back, shoulders and paws. They also use them to hunt and capture prey, to escape or defend against predators and as part of their marking behavior when they live outdoors. Cats are digitigrades, meaning they walk on their toes. Most other mammals, including humans, walk on the soles of their feet. item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Guava offers a wealth of health-promoting bioactive compounds, vitamins and minerals that both you and your pet can benefit from
  • One notable compound that’s specifically found in the guava plant and its parts is guaijaverin; it also contains quercetin, beta-carotene, lycopene, and ascorbic and citric acid
  • Guava is considered a rich source of pectin, a naturally occurring soluble fiber that may help improve pets’ gut health in various ways
  • Guava also contains quercetin, which exerts a wide array of biological activities, such as antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiallergy, antiarthritic, neuroprotective and wound-healing properties
  • You can use guava as an ingredient to your pet’s homemade treats or as a meal topper to diversify their species-appropriate, nutritionally balanced diet

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published March 21, 2024.

Often enjoyed in smoothies, jams, pastries and other confectionery creations, guava (Psidium guajava) is a tropical fruit that’s known for its sweet, juicy flesh, which smells musky and pungent when ripe. It’s also a delectable treat when eaten fresh, and if you’re wondering whether you can share it with your pet, the short answer is yes. Continue reading to learn more benefits of guava for your furry friend and how you can make it a healthy addition to their species-appropriate, nutritionally balanced diet.

Guava Fun Fact

Guava is also referred to as the “poor man’s apple of the tropics” because it has a similar shape to apples, but is more affordable and widely available in tropical regions.1,2

What Is Guava and How Does It Benefit Pet Health?

A member of the Myrtaceae plant family,3 guava is believed to have originated from Mexico, Central America, South America and the Caribbean, and is now grown in many tropical and subtropical areas around the world.4 The fruit comes in different colors and sizes, with pink guava being the most well-known variety. However, there are around 30 different types of red and white guavas that are either round or oval, as well as one variant of yellow-fleshed guava developed in California.5

This fruit is sometimes named after its flavor profile. One example is the strawberry guava, which tastes reminiscent of strawberries, and the lemon guava, which is tart and lemony.6 Regardless of variety, guava offers a wealth of health-promoting bioactive compounds, vitamins and minerals that both you and your pet can benefit from. It also has a long history of use in various therapeutic applications. According to an article published in Clinical Phytoscience:7

“Many countries have a long history of using guava for medicinal purposes. This plant finds applications for the treatment of diarrhea, dysentery, gastroenteritis, hypertension, diabetes, caries and pain relief and for improvement in locomotors coordination …
Its fruit is rich in vitamins A, C, iron, phosphorus and calcium and minerals. It contains high content of organic and inorganic compounds like secondary metabolites e.g. antioxidants, polyphenols, antiviral compounds, anti-inflammatory compounds.”

Did You Know?

Guavas offer more vitamin C than oranges. A 100-gram guava fruit has 228 milligrams of vitamin C8 — that’s almost four times the amount of vitamin C found in 100 grams of oranges.9 Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that dogs and cats can produce in their own body via their liver,10 but obtaining additional amounts of it from fresh foods like guava is also good for their health.

Guava Offers Various Health-Promoting Phytochemicals

Guavas offers a wide array of bioactive compounds. One notable compound that’s specifically found in the guava plant and its fruit is guaijaverin, which research shows may have a high potential as an antiplaque agent, as it helps inhibit the growth of bacteria in the mouth.11

Guava also contains quercetin, which exerts a wide array of biological activities, such as antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiallergy, antiarthritic, neuroprotective and wound-healing properties.12 According to a study published in the journal Veterinary Sciences, quercetin helped stimulate the immune response in dogs.13

Guava is high in ascorbic acid and citric acid as well, which are the major compounds that play important role in this fruit’s antimutagenic activity.14 Plus, it’s a good source of beta-carotene (provitamin A) and lycopene,15 both of which are carotenoids that exert potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and chemopreventive properties.16 They also help support your pet’s eye health by protecting against oxidative stress and age-related eye diseases.17

Guava Provides Gut-Healthy Pectin

“Guava is considered a rich source of pectin, a naturally occurring soluble fiber that may help improve pets’ gut health in various ways.”

One of pectin’s mechanisms of action is by promoting the production of short-chain fatty acids, which in turn support your pet’s intestinal epithelium and aid in meeting their energy requirements.18

According to an article published in Frontiers in Microbiology, pectin also helps “induce gut immunity, improve intestinal integrity and mucosal proliferation, and favor adhesion of probiotic Lactobacillus strains to the epithelial cells.”19 A study published in the Journal of Animal Science showed similar results, demonstrating that higher pectin intake helped increase the C. perfringens and lactobacilli concentration in cats.20

How to Choose and Safely Offer Guava to Your Pet

Fresh guava is available in most supermarkets in Florida and nearby areas, or in special grocery stores around the country. When buying guava, gently squeeze the fruit to gauge if it’s ripe; softer guavas are riper and sweeter. The skin should also be lighter in color, sometimes with spots of pink. Dark green peel indicates that they’re not as ripe; you can speed up their ripening by putting them in a bowl or a paper bag and leaving them at room temperature in the kitchen.21

Ripe guavas are highly perishable, so if you’re not going to eat them or feed them to your pet right away, store them in the fridge first to slow down the ripening process. Once you’re ready to offer it to your pet, cut the flesh into bite-sized pieces to avoid choking risks, and remove the seeds. You can either remove the peel or leave it on (if organic), as it’s edible and contains high amounts of the phytochemicals mentioned above. Always remove the stem prior to feeding.

You can use ripe guava as an ingredient to your pet’s homemade treats or as a meal topper to diversify their food bowl. You can also puree it and spread it on your pet’s lick mat. As always, remember to limit the serving of healthy “extras,” including guava, to less than 10% of your pet’s daily caloric intake. Avoid feeding your pet processed guava products like jams and jellies, as they contain excessive amounts of sugar.

Top Producers of Guava in the US and Globally

According to data from the Food and Agriculture Organization, India leads the world’s guava production, accounting for 39% of the global output. Second place goes to Pakistan, with 14% of global output, while Brazil ranks third at 7% of global output.22 In the U.S., guava is primarily grown in Florida, California and Hawaii.23

Is Guava a Sustainable Crop?

According to HeaLabel, guava is a relatively sustainable crop. Guava has a low water footprint, requiring only 1,800 liters of water to produce 1 kilogram of guava fruit.24 Guava trees are drought-tolerant, although they will produce a better yield if they have access to water.25 Guava’s carbon footprint is also relatively low, as it only takes about 0.15 kg CO2e to produce 1 kilogram of fresh guava, which is equivalent to a car driving 0.75 kilometers.26

Guava is also not included in the Environmental Working Group’s Dirty Dozen list, so conventionally grown varieties may have minimal to no pesticide residues and may be safe to eat. But to make sure that the guava you’re serving to your family, including your pets, is truly safe and sustainable, opt for spray-free, organic varieties at your local farmers market whenever possible.

item.title: The Human Procedure That Could Give Your Sick Dog a Normal Life
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The first pacemaker implanted in a dog was in 1967, and the patient was a 10-year-old Basenji with recurrent congestive heart failure
  • Pacemakers are placed in dogs with life-threatening arrhythmias, as well as dogs with heart conditions that impact their quality of life
  • Three canine heart conditions that can benefit from a pacemaker include sick sinus syndrome, atrial standstill and advanced atrioventricular block
  • Specific nutraceuticals and other adjunctive therapies are also recommended to support cardiac health, even in dogs with electrical problems of the heart
  • Dogs typically need about a month of rest after pacemaker placement and should switch from a collar to a harness to avoid pressure on the neck

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published December 13, 2017.

There are many medical procedures that have crossed over from human to veterinary medicine, and one of them involves a lifesaving device you’ve likely heard of — the pacemaker.

Cardiologists have been implanting pacemakers in humans for over 50 years. These adjunctive therapies may help nourish and support overall heart health, reducing the likelihood of congestive heart failure over time. Interestingly, acupuncture (yes, there's a heart meridian!) may also benefit these patients.

item.title: Is Their Water Bowl Hiding a Surprising Upgrade?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Hydrogen water is regular water infused with dissolved molecular hydrogen gas, the smallest molecule in existence, which acts as a selective antioxidant that neutralizes only the most damaging free radicals without disrupting normal cell function
  • A 2021 study in beagles found dogs drinking hydrogen-rich water healed wounds in 19 days versus 22 days for controls, with better tissue vascularization and elevated antioxidant enzyme activity
  • Research and integrative veterinary practice point to potential benefits for wound healing, joint comfort, cognitive support in senior pets, gut health, coat quality, and athletic recovery in active dogs
  • Recommended starting doses are 1 to 2 milliliters (ml) per kilogram daily for dogs and 0.5 to 1 ml per kilogram for cats, introduced gradually alongside regular water rather than replacing it entirely
  • Skip or check with a vet first for pets undergoing chemotherapy, on diuretics, with congestive heart failure, immediately post-surgery, under eight weeks old, or cats with chronic kidney disease

You've done the research on pet food. You've thought about supplements. You've even upgraded to a nicer stainless-steel dish. But have you ever given a thought to the water going into their bowl?

Most pet parents haven't given it a second thought beyond using filtered water. And yet a small but growing body of veterinary and integrative health research suggests there's a surprisingly simple upgrade happening in some kitchens right now — one that might do more for your pet's joints, healing, and even aging brain than most of the pricier supplements on the shelf.

What Hydrogen Water Actually Is

Hydrogen water is regular water (H₂O) with additional dissolved molecular hydrogen gas (H₂), which is the smallest molecule in existence. Not to be confused with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), which is toxic, molecular hydrogen is an odorless, colorless, nontoxic gas that dissolves into water and behaves as a selective antioxidant once inside the body.

The therapeutic range studied in animals is roughly 0.5 to 1.6 parts per million (500 to 1,600 parts per billion) of dissolved H₂. What makes it interesting is how the molecule behaves in the body. Because it's so small, it slips through cellular membranes and can reach places where most conventional antioxidants can't, including the mitochondria, cell nuclei, and even brain tissue.

And rather than neutralizing every free radical in sight (which can cause its own problems), molecular hydrogen selectively scavenges the most damaging reactive oxygen species, specifically hydroxyl radicals and peroxynitrite, while leaving the beneficial signaling oxidation processes alone. Excess hydrogen simply exhales out through the lungs.1,2

Why Antioxidants Matter for Your Pet

Dogs and cats live in the same environmental soup we do. They breathe the same indoor air, walk on treated lawns, share exposure to household chemicals, and eat processed foods that generate reactive oxygen species during metabolism. Their built-in antioxidant defenses — enzymes like superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase — gradually weaken with age.

That imbalance between free radicals and antioxidant capacity is what scientists call oxidative stress, and it's implicated in almost every chronic condition in aging pets: arthritis, cognitive decline, cardiovascular changes, cancer, kidney disease, and more.3,4

Anything that can gently support the body's antioxidant systems over the years your pet is with you is worth understanding. Hydrogen water is one of the more scientifically grounded options in the current pet wellness space.

What Research Actually Shows

The most rigorous pet-specific study on hydrogen water to date came out in 2021 in the journal Veterinary Sciences. Researchers worked with twelve male beagle dogs, created standardized skin wounds, and gave one group four hundred milliliters (ml) of hydrogen-rich water three times daily while the control group drank standard distilled water.5

The results were meaningful across every metric. The dogs drinking hydrogen water healed their wounds in an average of 19 days versus 22 days for the control group. At the 7-day mark, wound closure was 46.8% in the hydrogen group versus just 16.4% in the control group.

The tissue under a microscope showed significantly greater blood vessel density, which is what healing tissues need for oxygen and nutrient delivery. Biochemically, hydrogen water raised levels of SOD (superoxide dismutase) — an important antioxidant enzyme — and lowered markers of oxidative damage. It also activated the Nrf2 signaling pathway, which upregulates the body's own antioxidant defenses. And no adverse effects were reported throughout the study.6

Beyond that specific study, a large body of animal research — including hundreds of studies reviewed in a 2024 comprehensive review in Biochemistry and Biophysics Reports — supports molecular hydrogen's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects across multiple mammalian systems.7 Studies in rodent models have shown reductions in hippocampal oxidative stress, improved cognitive performance in age-related decline, reduced markers of periodontal (gum and dental) damage, and reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6.8

Where the Benefits May Show Up in Your Pet

Based on the current research, hydrogen water may support a surprisingly wide range of everyday pet health concerns. The common thread across almost all of them is the same mechanism — reducing oxidative stress and calming low-grade inflammation before they can start to compound over the years.

  • Wound healing and post-surgical recovery — The strongest pet-specific research evidence links hydrogen water to faster wound closure and better tissue regeneration.9
  • Joint comfort and mobility — Molecular hydrogen's anti-inflammatory action may reduce the oxidative damage that drives arthritis and stiffness in aging dogs and cats.10
  • Cognitive support in senior pets — Canine Cognitive Dysfunction Syndrome affects roughly 28% of dogs aged 11 to 12 and over 68% of dogs aged 15 to 16. Hydrogen's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and reduce oxidative stress in brain tissue is why some integrative vets believe that hydrogen may have healing potential for CCD.11
  • Gut health and immune support — Reduced intestinal oxidative stress and modulated immune responses — may be potentially relevant for pets with inflammatory bowel disease or food sensitivities.12
  • Coat and skin quality — The connection between oxidative stress and skin barrier function makes this a biologically plausible benefit, though controlled studies specifically on coat and skin health are lacking.13
  • Athletic recovery for active dogs — Studies on performance animals — including horses in competitive racing — have shown reduced muscle inflammation and lower blood lactate levels after intense exercise.14
  • Quality of life in older pets — Reduced anxiety, better mood, and improved nerve function have all been noted in human studies, and integrative vets increasingly extrapolate these to aging pets.15

How to Actually Give It

Introducing hydrogen water is simple, but a few practical notes matter — mostly because dissolved hydrogen behaves a little differently than any other supplement you might offer, and small mistakes in preparation or delivery can cancel out most of the benefits.

  • Start low, go slow — A conservative starting dose for dogs is 1 to 2 ml per kilogram of body weight per day. For cats, 0.5 to 1 ml per kilogram. Introduce it at about 25% of the target amount and build up over one to two weeks. Watch for any digestive changes as your pet adjusts.16
  • Don't replace all their water — Hydrogen water supplements the normal water bowl rather than replacing it entirely. This is especially important for cats, who can be stressed by abrupt changes to their drinking environment. Many pet parents offer hydrogen water in a separate bowl alongside their regular water and let their cat decide.
  • Fresh is best — Dissolved hydrogen begins off-gassing immediately after production. At room temperature in an open bowl, most of it dissipates within 30 to 60 minutes. Prepare hydrogen water close to serving time and offer it right after generating. In sealed containers, it holds for a few hours.
  • Morning delivery works well — Giving hydrogen water on an empty stomach in the morning appears to support the best absorption.
  • Monitor — Mild, temporary increases in urination can happen as the body responds to the antioxidant support. That's usually not a concern. Persistent digestive upset warrants discontinuing use and checking with your vet.

Choosing a Device Worth Trusting

Not all hydrogen water products are created equal. The quality of the technology directly affects how much dissolved hydrogen your pet receives and whether harmful byproducts get in along the way. Here are factors to look for:

  • Solid Polymer Electrolyte/Proton Exchange Membrane (SPE/PEM) technology — SPE/PEM electrolysis separates the electrolysis cell so that ozone and chlorine (toxic byproducts produced at the anode) are drained away separately. Single-chamber devices cannot separate these contaminants.
  • Platinum-coated titanium electrodes — This is the industry standard. They don't corrode, don't leach metals, and maintain consistent hydrogen production over time.
  • Verified PPB output — The device should specify its output in parts per billion or parts per million, ideally verified by independent laboratory testing rather than just manufacturer claims.
  • Third-party certifications — Look for International Hydrogen Standards Association (IHSA) certification and H₂ Analytics testing.
  • FDA-registered manufacturing facilities — are recommended for the device components that contact water.

Portable hydrogen water bottles work well for daily use and for taking on hikes or trips. Countertop pitchers or jugs are convenient for multi-pet households or families who also drink hydrogen water themselves. Regular carbon filters and reverse osmosis systems do not produce hydrogen water — you need a specific device that generates and dissolves molecular hydrogen. Hydrogen tablets exist too but tend to produce less predictable concentrations.17

When to Skip It or Ask Your Vet First

Hydrogen water has a strong safety profile, and no serious adverse events have been reported across human or animal studies. But there are situations that warrant extra caution or veterinary conversation before introducing it:18

  • Pets undergoing chemotherapy — Hydrogen's antioxidant effects could theoretically interfere with the effectiveness of chemotherapy. Talk to your veterinary oncologist first.
  • Pets on diuretic medications — Any increase in fluid intake could alter dosing or hydration status.
  • Pets with congestive heart failure — Increased fluid intake can be harmful for heart failure cases, so monitor your pet closely.
  • Immediately post-major surgery — Although it assists in wound healing, contact your vet to make sure it is safe for your pet’s particular surgery.
  • Young animals (under eight weeks) — Puppies and kittens should stick with species-appropriate milk or plain water during this window.
  • Cats with chronic kidney disease — May benefit from hydrogen water's antioxidant support (since oxidative stress drives CKD progression), but reduced fluid intake can be harmful for cats with kidney disease so monitor your pet closely.

For all pets, an integrative or holistic veterinarian who's familiar with hydrogen therapy is the best person to help decide whether it makes sense for your specific animal, especially if they are on medications or have chronic health conditions.

Honest Limits of the Science

It would be misleading to present hydrogen water as fully established therapy. The evidence base is promising but still developing. However, it’s worth acknowledging that most animal research has been short-term — days to weeks rather than years. Long-term multi-year safety data specifically in cats and dogs is still lacking.

Species-specific dosing standards haven't been formally published by major veterinary associations yet. Condition-specific efficacy trials in dogs and cats — for arthritis, IBD, CKD, cognitive decline — are limited compared to the human literature. And some of the more enthusiastic claims in the online pet wellness space run ahead of what the evidence supports currently.

None of that means hydrogen water is ineffective. The scientific evidence is solid, the safety data is reassuring, and the 2021 study provides real proof of concept. But it does mean hydrogen water should be viewed as a supportive tool in a comprehensive wellness plan — not a stand-alone treatment for diagnosed disease. Your pet's diet, their environment, their exercise, and their overall care all matter more than any single supplement, including this one.

What to Watch For

Since pets can't tell you how they feel, watch for these signals over four to eight weeks of consistent use:

  • Increased energy or playfulness, especially in senior pets
  • Reduced stiffness after sleep or rest
  • Improved coat sheen and less dry, flaky skin
  • More regular digestion
  • Calmer demeanor in anxious pets
  • Faster healing of minor cuts, scrapes, or post-operative incisions

If you see no meaningful change after eight to 12 weeks of consistent, properly dosed use, hydrogen water may simply not be the right intervention for your specific pet, and that's useful information too.19

The Real Takeaway

Water is the one thing your pet drinks every single day of their life. That daily volume over their lifetime, adds up to a big opportunity to deliver something beneficial through a simple intervention. Hydrogen water represents one of the more scientifically grounded ways to make that daily bowl of water do a little more work — supporting antioxidant defenses, calming inflammation, and helping tissues heal a little faster.

It's not a miracle and it is not a replacement for a good diet, regular holistic vet care, exercise, or the many other pieces of a well-rounded wellness plan. But for aging pets dealing with joint stiffness or cognitive changes, active dogs needing better recovery, or pets healing from surgery or injury, it's a low-risk addition that a growing number of integrative and holistic veterinarians are watching closely. The research is still evolving. The safety profile is reassuring. And the setup is genuinely as simple as swapping a bottle of water.

Your pet's water bowl has been sitting quietly on the kitchen floor for years. It might be time to take a second look at what's actually in it.

Sources and References

  • 1,8,12,13,16,18,19 Purepebrix, February 28, 2026
  • 2,3,10,14,17 Ion Bottles, April 1, 2026
  • 4,15 Rallie, April 1, 2022
  • 5,6,9 Vet Sci. 2021 Nov 4;8(11):264
  • 7 Biochem Biophys Rep. 2025 Jan 25;41:101933. doi: 10.1016/j.bbrep.2025.101933
  • 11 Curr Alzheimer Res. 2018 Mar 14;15(5):482-492

  • Gut health and immune support — Reduced intestinal oxidative stress and modulated immune responses — may be potentially relevant for pets with inflammatory bowel disease or food sensitivities.12
  • Coat and skin quality — The connection between oxidative stress and skin barrier function makes this a biologically plausible benefit, though controlled studies specifically on coat and skin health are lacking.13
  • Athletic recovery for active dogs — Studies on performance animals — including horses in competitive racing — have shown reduced muscle inflammation and lower blood lactate levels after intense exercise.14
  • Quality of life in older pets — Reduced anxiety, better mood, and improved nerve function have all been noted in human studies, and integrative vets increasingly extrapolate these to aging pets.15

How to Actually Give It

Introducing hydrogen water is simple, but a few practical notes matter — mostly because dissolved hydrogen behaves a little differently than any other supplement you might offer, and small mistakes in preparation or delivery can cancel out most of the benefits.

  • Start low, go slow — A conservative starting dose for dogs is 1 to 2 ml per kilogram of body weight per day. For cats, 0.5 to 1 ml per kilogram. Introduce it at about 25% of the target amount and build up over one to two weeks. Watch for any digestive changes as your pet adjusts.16
  • Don't replace all their water — Hydrogen water supplements the normal water bowl rather than replacing it entirely. This is especially important for cats, who can be stressed by abrupt changes to their drinking environment. Many pet parents offer hydrogen water in a separate bowl alongside their regular water and let their cat decide.
  • Fresh is best — Dissolved hydrogen begins off-gassing immediately after production. At room temperature in an open bowl, most of it dissipates within 30 to 60 minutes. Prepare hydrogen water close to serving time and offer it right after generating. In sealed containers, it holds for a few hours.
  • Morning delivery works well — Giving hydrogen water on an empty stomach in the morning appears to support the best absorption.
  • Monitor — Mild, temporary increases in urination can happen as the body responds to the antioxidant support. That's usually not a concern. Persistent digestive upset warrants discontinuing use and checking with your vet.

Choosing a Device Worth Trusting

Not all hydrogen water products are created equal. The quality of the technology directly affects how much dissolved hydrogen your pet receives and whether harmful byproducts get in along the way. Here are factors to look for:

  • Solid Polymer Electrolyte/Proton Exchange Membrane (SPE/PEM) technology — SPE/PEM electrolysis separates the electrolysis cell so that ozone and chlorine (toxic byproducts produced at the anode) are drained away separately. Single-chamber devices cannot separate these contaminants.
  • Platinum-coated titanium electrodes — This is the industry standard. They don't corrode, don't leach metals, and maintain consistent hydrogen production over time.
  • Verified PPB output — The device should specify its output in parts per billion or parts per million, ideally verified by independent laboratory testing rather than just manufacturer claims.
  • Third-party certifications — Look for International Hydrogen Standards Association (IHSA) certification and H₂ Analytics testing.
  • FDA-registered manufacturing facilities — are recommended for the device components that contact water.

Portable hydrogen water bottles work well for daily use and for taking on hikes or trips. Countertop pitchers or jugs are convenient for multi-pet households or families who also drink hydrogen water themselves. Regular carbon filters and reverse osmosis systems do not produce hydrogen water — you need a specific device that generates and dissolves molecular hydrogen. Hydrogen tablets exist too but tend to produce less predictable concentrations.17

When to Skip It or Ask Your Vet First

Hydrogen water has a strong safety profile, and no serious adverse events have been reported across human or animal studies. But there are situations that warrant extra caution or veterinary conversation before introducing it:18

  • Pets undergoing chemotherapy — Hydrogen's antioxidant effects could theoretically interfere with the effectiveness of chemotherapy. Talk to your veterinary oncologist first.
  • Pets on diuretic medications — Any increase in fluid intake could alter dosing or hydration status.
  • Pets with congestive heart failure — Increased fluid intake can be harmful for heart failure cases, so monitor your pet closely.
  • Immediately post-major surgery — Although it assists in wound healing, contact your vet to make sure it is safe for your pet’s particular surgery.
  • Young animals (under eight weeks) — Puppies and kittens should stick with species-appropriate milk or plain water during this window.
  • Cats with chronic kidney disease — May benefit from hydrogen water's antioxidant support (since oxidative stress drives CKD progression), but reduced fluid intake can be harmful for cats with kidney disease so monitor your pet closely.

For all pets, an integrative or holistic veterinarian who's familiar with hydrogen therapy is the best person to help decide whether it makes sense for your specific animal, especially if they are on medications or have chronic health conditions.

Honest Limits of the Science

It would be misleading to present hydrogen water as fully established therapy. The evidence base is promising but still developing. However, it’s worth acknowledging that most animal research has been short-term — days to weeks rather than years. Long-term multi-year safety data specifically in cats and dogs is still lacking.

Species-specific dosing standards haven't been formally published by major veterinary associations yet. Condition-specific efficacy trials in dogs and cats — for arthritis, IBD, CKD, cognitive decline — are limited compared to the human literature. And some of the more enthusiastic claims in the online pet wellness space run ahead of what the evidence supports currently.

None of that means hydrogen water is ineffective. The scientific evidence is solid, the safety data is reassuring, and the 2021 study provides real proof of concept. But it does mean hydrogen water should be viewed as a supportive tool in a comprehensive wellness plan — not a stand-alone treatment for diagnosed disease. Your pet's diet, their environment, their exercise, and their overall care all matter more than any single supplement, including this one.

What to Watch For

Since pets can't tell you how they feel, watch for these signals over four to eight weeks of consistent use:

  • Increased energy or playfulness, especially in senior pets
  • Reduced stiffness after sleep or rest
  • Improved coat sheen and less dry, flaky skin
  • More regular digestion
  • Calmer demeanor in anxious pets
  • Faster healing of minor cuts, scrapes, or post-operative incisions

If you see no meaningful change after eight to 12 weeks of consistent, properly dosed use, hydrogen water may simply not be the right intervention for your specific pet, and that's useful information too.19

The Real Takeaway

Water is the one thing your pet drinks every single day of their life. That daily volume over their lifetime, adds up to a big opportunity to deliver something beneficial through a simple intervention. Hydrogen water represents one of the more scientifically grounded ways to make that daily bowl of water do a little more work — supporting antioxidant defenses, calming inflammation, and helping tissues heal a little faster.

It's not a miracle and it is not a replacement for a good diet, regular holistic vet care, exercise, or the many other pieces of a well-rounded wellness plan. But for aging pets dealing with joint stiffness or cognitive changes, active dogs needing better recovery, or pets healing from surgery or injury, it's a low-risk addition that a growing number of integrative and holistic veterinarians are watching closely. The research is still evolving. The safety profile is reassuring. And the setup is genuinely as simple as swapping a bottle of water.

Your pet's water bowl has been sitting quietly on the kitchen floor for years. It might be time to take a second look at what's actually in it.
